analysis.one_liner: Requires a license and background check to own or buy a gun and bans assault weapons.
analysis.headline: A sweeping gun regulation bill with 21 cosponsors never received a hearing or vote, dying in a House subcommittee when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every gun and ammunition owner to get a federal license after a background check and safety training, extended background checks to private sales, raised the purchase age to 21, created a court process for families to temporarily remove guns from someone in crisis, banned semiautomatic assault weapons and silencers, stripped gun makers of their shield from lawsuits, let the Consumer Product Safety Commission set gun safety standards, raised federal gun taxes, and funded community violence intervention programs and gun violence research. It was referred to three committees, sent to a Judiciary subcommittee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to gun violence: households facing domestic abusers and stalkers, communities hit by gun trafficking, and victims of mass shootings. It would also fund local violence intervention programs and, for the first time in decades, government research on gun violence.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to gun violence and abuse

how_it_helps.text: It requires a federal firearm owner's license — age 21, safety training, background check, photo — to buy or possess a gun or ammunition, with a dealer-verifiable licensing database [S2][S3].

It closes the private-sale loophole by requiring a licensed dealer to run a background check before virtually any private transfer, and extends the background-check waiting period from three to seven business days [S2][S3].

It expands the list of people barred from having guns to include stalkers and people under restraining orders for harassing an intimate partner, closing gaps that leave dating partners and stalking victims unprotected [S3].

It lets family members or police ask a federal court for an extreme risk protection order to temporarily remove guns from someone posing a danger, with notice, a hearing, counsel for the person, and a 180-day limit on orders [S2][S3].

It restricts assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, bans ghost guns and silencers, makes firearms trafficking a stand-alone crime, and funds community violence intervention grants and gun violence research [S2].

It repeals the law that shields gun manufacturers from most civil lawsuits and lets the Consumer Product Safety Commission issue safety standards for firearms, gun locks, and safes — the same product-safety regime every other consumer product answers to [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Lawful gun owners, who would need a license, training, and safe storage to keep guns and would pay higher excise taxes passed through by manufacturers; and the gun industry — manufacturers facing lawsuits and new product regulation, dealers facing security plans, inspections, and record-keeping rules, and silencer and assault-weapon makers facing a ban on their products.

drawbacks.text: The licensing requirement makes unlicensed possession of a gun or ammunition a crime carrying up to two years in prison, so millions of otherwise lawful owners would have to obtain a license, complete testing, and pay fees or become criminals — and the exception for guns already owned means the rules bind new buyers most heavily [S3].

The bill bans the manufacture, sale, and possession of a broad category of semiautomatic firearms and silencers and extends gun-free school zones to colleges with no exception for licensed carriers, restrictions critics call overbroad and likely to sweep in common hunting and sporting rifles [S2][S3].

Seven-day waiting periods, safe-storage penalties, and licensing costs fall hardest on rural owners, people who keep a gun for self-defense, and lower-income buyers, and the excise tax increase would raise the price of every gun and its ammunition [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety benefits — universal background checks, licensing, domestic-violence and stalking protections, a trafficking offense, and funding for violence intervention — are the kind of measures with broad public support, and the bill built in due process for its most intrusive tools, like court hearings and counsel for people subject to gun-removal orders. The real cost is the burden placed on lawful gun owners: a nationwide license-to-own regime, a weapons ban, higher taxes, and criminal penalties for noncompliance, whose effectiveness depends entirely on federal and state agencies actually administering the system. The bill is ambitious rather than finely balanced, and its breadth — it touches nearly every part of federal gun law — made it a maximalist opening position rather than a narrow fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then to a Judiciary subcommittee, and sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Representative Hank Johnson of Georgia introduced the bill on January 30, 2020, with 16 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means committees [S5].
On March 10, 2020, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security — the last action ever taken on it [S5].
It ended the Congress with 21 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote in either chamber [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and silencer and assault-weapon makers avoided a licensing regime, lawsuit liability, product regulation, and higher taxes, and lawful gun owners avoided the license and storage mandates.

for.name: Rep. Henry C. 'Hank' Johnson Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 21 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored.

against.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
against.role: Chair, House Judiciary Committee (the committee of primary referral)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a subcommittee or full-committee markup; it sat in the Crime subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; the record shows no rule, vote, or scheduling action on it.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as a national gun registry and owner-licensing scheme and mobilized opposition to gun-control legislation generally.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported it; with Democrats holding a 231-seat House majority, the bill still never reached a hearing or vote, and the Senate, then run by Republicans, was never a factor.

industries.note: The bill repeals the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act liability shield, lets the CPSC regulate firearms as consumer products, raises excise taxes, and bans a core product line (assault weapons and silencers). The bill's premise is that these products' unregulated sale endangers the public, so the industry's interest in keeping liability protection and an unregulated market runs against the bill's safety goals.

Dealers would face mandatory security plans to deter theft, employee background checks, enhanced record-keeping and inspections, and lost/stolen reporting duties, plus a new role running background checks on all private sales. These are compliance costs the industry has long resisted, though the dealer-verification database also formalizes dealers' gatekeeper position in every sale.

The licensing, training, safe-storage, and tax provisions raise costs for millions of lawful owners and the retailers serving them; the bill's exceptions for existing guns, hunting, and family transfers soften but do not remove that burden.
